posts.central_knowledge_unit: Ulama, a 3,400-year-old ballgame that survived in Mexico | AP News
posts.claim: Ulama de cadera is a living Sinaloan form of the Mesoamerican rubber-ball tradition. It is played with a heavy solid rubber ball struck with the hip (sources also describe the upper thigh) and protective gear; Mexican and scholarly sources characterize it as a survival of, or closely related to, the pre-Hispanic ballgame. Archaeology supports a Mesoamerican ballgame by about 1650 BCE, but does not establish that modern ulama’s rules have remained unchanged or continuously documented for 3,400 years, nor that it is definitively the world’s oldest team sport.
posts.headline: Ulama: Ancient Mexican Hip‑Ball Game Endures After Millennia

posts.claim: The ballgame represents one of the most enduring and iconic features of ancient Mesoamerican civilization, yet its origins and evolution remain poorly understood, primarily associated with the Gulf Coast and southern Pacific coastal lowlands. While one early ballcourt dates to 1650 BCE from the Chiapas lowlands, ballcourts have remained undocumented in the Mesoamerican highlands until a millennium later, suggesting less involvement by highland civilizations in the ballgame’s evolution.
